clue.text: Putting a barbarian in goal could be the last place to put him!

definitions.text: the last place to put him

indicators.note: 'could be' says the combined letters might become something else once rearranged

blocks.note: the Goths were the archetypal barbarian tribe
taken as written

explanation.surface: A football joke: sticking a hulking barbarian in goal would be the last resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' sounds like a container signal, but the two words are simply mixed together. The definition is cryptic: Golgotha, the hill of the Crucifixion, is where Christ was finally put.
explanation.definitionFit: Golgotha was the hill outside Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified, so it was his final earthly resting place before burial.

clue.text: Avon, I see, could be arcadian for Adam

blocks.note: the Prime Minister Anthony Eden was made Earl of Avon
the two letters spoken one after the other

explanation.surface: Someone gazing at the River Avon and calling it idyllic, a paradise fit for Adam.
explanation.walkthrough: Avon looks like the river; here it is Anthony Eden's title as Earl of Avon. The letters I and C read out sound like 'I see'.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam lived in the Garden of Eden, so a place idyllic and paradisal in his terms would be Edenic.

clue.text: Mean to go into denial with this game supplier

indicators.note: one word is told to enter another, so it sits inside it

blocks.note: the word of refusal
to mean to do something is to intend it

explanation.surface: A games company accused of refusing to admit something, perhaps a fault in its consoles.
explanation.definitionFit: Nintendo is the Japanese company that makes video game consoles and software such as Mario and Zelda.

clue.text: Modern little woman at home with neighbour

blocks.note: Anno Domini, the current era
Jo March is one of Louisa May Alcott's Little Women
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: A modern housewife spending her days at home with the woman next door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little woman' looks like a dated phrase for a wife; it points to Jo of Alcott's Little Women.
explanation.definitionFit: Neighbour works as a verb here: two things that neighbour each other lie side by side, touching, which is to adjoin.

clue.text: (and 6) Awkward and unsighted without retracting my d***** specs

indicators.note: to retract is to draw back, so the words that follow are read in the backward direction
'without' in its old sense of outside, so one word wraps around the others

blocks.note: taken as written
the swear word is printed as its first letter only
two round lenses look like a pair of letter Os
someone unsighted has been blinded

explanation.surface: Someone swearing because they cannot see properly without their wretched glasses.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs across 5 and 6. The asterisks bleep a swear word, leaving only its initial; the backward run of three pieces goes in after the first two letters of the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: Bloody-minded is British slang for deliberately obstructive and uncooperative, the same as being awkward on purpose.

clue.text: (and 16) Show disapproval, that is, among women go-go dancing. That's some rhythm!

indicators.note: letters that are dancing move around and change places
one thing among others is placed in their midst

blocks.note: the jeer of an unhappy audience
the standard abbreviation
taken as written
id est, Latin for that is
that is again, abbreviated in the same way

explanation.surface: Booing a troupe of go-go dancers and then admitting that they have got rhythm.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs across 5 and 16 down. IE goes among the shuffled W and GOGO, giving GIEWOOG; the closing 'That's' supplies the final IE, so the clue does double duty.
explanation.definitionFit: Boogie-woogie is a fast blues piano style built on a driving repeated bass rhythm, so it is one kind of rhythm.

clue.text: See 5
(and 17) Herr Rassendyll?

blocks.note: surface reading: a German gentleman with an odd surname
setter's reading: Rudolf Rassendyll, the Englishman in The Prisoner of Zenda who is the exact double of the King of Ruritania; Herr asks for the German word

explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs across 7 and 17 down. Rassendyll impersonates the king he looks just like, and 'Herr' tells you the word wanted is German.
explanation.definitionFit: A doppelganger is an uncanny lookalike or double of a living person, which is exactly what Rassendyll is to the Ruritanian king.

clue.text: Chucker-out of children held in suspense here?

blocks.note: first meaning, playful: a bouncer who throws out babies, as a nightclub bouncer throws out drunks
second meaning: a sprung harness in which an infant hangs and bobs up and down

explanation.surface: A nursery thriller in which the children are kept on tenterhooks by a bouncer.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are whimsical: a bouncer is a doorman who ejects people, and suspense is used literally for being suspended.
explanation.definitionFit: A baby bouncer is a seat or harness hung from a spring or doorframe, keeping an infant literally suspended off the floor.

clue.text: No booze for Jack Turner's ugly sister

indicators.note: a turner turns things round, so the preceding words face the other way

blocks.note: taken as written
grog is the watered rum issued to sailors, and Jack Tar is a sailor

explanation.surface: A pantomime line: the Ugly Sister played by Jack Turner gets no drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack Turner' reads as an actor's name. Jack is the sailor, and Turner's tells you to turn the letters round.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gorgons were three monstrous sisters of Greek myth, Medusa among them, so hideous that a glance turned onlookers to stone.

clue.text: Seat of the Spencers east of this Trent-side village

blocks.note: Althorp is the Northamptonshire house of the Spencer family, Princess Diana's childhood home
the compass abbreviation

explanation.surface: Directions to the Spencers' stately home, lying east of a village on the River Trent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'East of' looks like a position on the map; E is simply added after the house's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Althorpe is a small village in North Lincolnshire standing on the bank of the River Trent, a river of the English Midlands.

clue.text: "The Soldier's Tale" starts with the Colonel, say?

definitions.note: say marks a sound-alike: Colonel is pronounced kernel

indicators.note: a word's start is its opening letter, which is all that is kept

blocks.note: a GI is an American soldier, with the possessive s
the opening letter

explanation.surface: Stravinsky's The Soldier's Tale beginning with the entrance of a colonel.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is itself a sound-alike: Colonel is said 'kernel', and the kernel of something is its essence.
explanation.definitionFit: The kernel of an argument is its central core, which is the gist; the military rank colonel is pronounced identically.

clue.text: Niobe's claim for attention?

blocks.note: surface reading: a tragic figure demanding to be noticed
setter's reading: Niobe wept endlessly for her slain children, so any appeal she made would come through tears

explanation.walkthrough: Niobe, in Greek myth, was turned to a stone that never stopped weeping. The phrase meaning an urgent requirement is read literally as a need expressed by weeping.
explanation.definitionFit: A pressing requirement that demands to be met is a desperate or urgent want, and Niobe's would be accompanied by tears.

clue.text: The apostle's mother-in-law sobs wildly, lacking in two saints

indicators.note: whatever is lacking is left out of the letters around it
letters behaving wildly fly out of their proper order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, to be removed
S is the abbreviation for saint, twice over

explanation.surface: A comic vignette: the disciple's mother-in-law weeping uncontrollably.
explanation.walkthrough: Strike IN and two Ss from mother-in-law sobs, then rearrange the remaining eleven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Bartholomew was one of the twelve disciples chosen by Jesus, often identified with Nathanael in John's gospel.

clue.text: Not following suit, can force hold the rear?

indicators.note: letters that hold something keep it within them

blocks.note: a tin is a can
g is the symbol for the force of gravity
the rump is the hindquarters

explanation.surface: A question about whether strength can keep an army's rearguard together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not following suit' is card-play language: a player with no card of the suit led may play a trump instead.
explanation.definitionFit: In whist or bridge, trumping means playing a card of the trump suit when unable to match the suit that was led.

clue.text: The Observer's remedy? Yes! One meal ticket between two Europeans

blocks.note: E for European, the first of the pair
taken as written
one is the indefinite article
a luncheon voucher, a British employee's meal ticket
the second E of the pair

explanation.surface: A newspaper advertisement promising a cure and a free lunch ticket for continental readers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Observer looks like the Sunday newspaper; it means anyone who observes, using their eyes. Luncheon vouchers were a British workplace perk, a meal ticket.
explanation.definitionFit: An eye salve is an ointment for sore eyes, so it is a remedy for the organs an observer relies upon.

clue.text: See 5
See 7
Adams's "Pihsretaw" thus folded?

blocks.note: Richard Adams wrote the rabbit novel Watership Down
the first word of that title written back to front, i.e. turned

explanation.surface: A garbled book title, as if a copy of the rabbit novel had been folded over and printed through.
explanation.walkthrough: Pihsretaw is Watership spelt backwards, so Adams's Down has been turned.
explanation.definitionFit: Something downturned has been turned or bent downwards, like a folded-over collar or the brim of a hat.

clue.text: Name the ass docked in infancy

indicators.note: a docked tail has been cut short, so the end comes off

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation
the onager is the wild ass of Asia

explanation.surface: Naming a donkey whose tail was cut when it was a foal.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonage is the legal term for being under age, a minority, and by extension early youth or childhood.

clue.text: Propped up to perform part of the service?

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom to the top

blocks.note: something propped is braced

explanation.surface: Someone propped up so they can take part in a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: The service is a car's, not a church's: a decarb is the old routine of scraping carbon from an engine.
explanation.definitionFit: Decarbonising the cylinders, a decarb, was once a regular task in a garage's routine maintenance of a car engine.

clue.text: Angeleno's place in point-to-point dash

indicators.note: one thing in another sits within it

blocks.note: two compass points, east and north
an Angeleno lives in Los Angeles

explanation.surface: A Los Angeles resident finding their place in an English point-to-point horse race.
explanation.walkthrough: A point-to-point is an amateur steeplechase in Britain, but here the points are compass directions.
explanation.definitionFit: Dash means flair and verve, a stylish energy, which is exactly the sense of the borrowed French word.

clue.text: Fount of inspiration needed after again failing PPE

indicators.note: an attempt that is failing goes wrong, so the letters come out in a muddle

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An Oxford student who flunked Philosophy, Politics and Economics again needs some inspiration.
explanation.walkthrough: PPE is the Oxford degree in Philosophy, Politics and Economics.
explanation.definitionFit: Aganippe was a spring on Mount Helicon sacred to the Muses, whose water was believed to inspire poets.

clue.text: The price of fish thrown back, say

indicators.note: what is thrown back goes the opposite way, so read right to left

blocks.note: the char is a fish of the trout family
e.g., for example, as 'say' is used

explanation.surface: Grumbling about the cost of fish, or the angler who throws the catch back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thrown back' seems to describe the fish; it actually turns the abbreviation for 'say' around.
explanation.definitionFit: A charge is the amount asked for goods or a service, the same as its price or fee.

clue.text: (and 25) One's on track with Verdi: "Green" in translation

indicators.note: translating changes a word's form, so these letters are recast into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A trivia note: Giuseppe Verdi translates into English as Joe Green.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs across 24 and 25. 'In translation' reads as one phrase, but 'in' belongs with the letters to be mixed and 'translation' alone signals the mixing.
explanation.definitionFit: An engine driver operates a railway locomotive, so his working life is spent on the track.

clue.text: See 24
